newsitem.title: UK: Crest head defends new share settlement system.
newsitem.headline: Crest head defends new share settlement system.

text.p: Iain Saville was at the Bank of England during Britain's crisis exit from the European exchange rate mechanism, yet he says leading the Crest project to automate London share matching is his toughest job ever.

As chief executive of CRESTCo, the Bank of England-led group developing a computerised share registration system, Saville is charged with ending a 17-year-old struggle to eliminate paper settlements at the London Stock Exchange (LSE).

On Monday, CRESTCo's 15-member board meets to consider postponing the April deadline to complete the transition to electronic settlements following software problems and complaints from some users of the system.
Postponing the deadline would be embarrassing for Crest, born from the ruins of Taurus, the LSE's earlier project to develop a computerised system for recording ownership of shares.

Saville, however, doesn't like to draw comparisons between Crest and Taurus. "They shouldn't even be mentioned in the same breath," he said on Friday. "When we're done, we'll have a state-of-the-art system."
Taurus was abandoned in 1993 after running up costs of 38 million pounds ($64 million), a debacle which led to the departure of the LSE's then chief executive Peter Rowlins.

In July, CRESTCo, a consortium of 60 financial institutions, launched the first leg of the transition to paperless settlements under Crest, after almost four years of development costing 29 million pounds. It was hailed as being on budget and on time.
But since its inauguration, Crest has experienced software and other problems, causing slow processing and huge backlogs of unmatched trades at Europe's busiest stock exchange.
Crest last month delayed the transfer of 10 stocks to sort out software bugs and now faces the possibility of another snag.

"From Crest's point of view, there's no argument to delay (the April deadline)," Saville told Reuters in an interview. "My personal view is that a sensible way to deal with it would be to wait and collect more data."
An option the board will discuss is adjusting tariffs to encourage use during off-peak hours so the system could manage greater volumes, one industry source said.

Saville calls Crest's difficulties "teething problems," but some settlement managers say the system isn't ready to handle larger volumes as the transition progresses to Crest from the LSE's existing system based on paper share certificates.

"It's a difficult political decision to make because it involves the Bank of England," said one settlement manager who asked not to be named. "But from a practical point of view, new entries (to Crest from Talisman) should be suspended for sometime longer than the month that (Crest) is proposing."
Current plans call for Crest to settle 43 percent of the market volume by the year end.
Saville said the main reason for last month's huge backlog and slow processing time was that too many messages were put in the system at once, and some were not sent properly.

He said some small brokerages had encountered difficulties with Crest because their own software was inadequate, but he declined to comment on the findings of regulators visiting the 243 participating firms.
"Everyone agrees the backlog is still larger than it should be.... but the reliablility of the system is absolutely 100 percent," Saville said.
Stephen Pinner, managing director at UK retail brokerage Cater Deal Services, said he had confidence in Crest's management and infrastructure, but said the system was too slow.
"The blame shouldn't be laid at the door of CRESTCo. That's just an easy cop out," Pinner said. "There are still problems with Crest, but there are problems with some of the firms too."
